# Reward Shaping

The task in [[it-applications-in-business-and-commerce]] is "drive a fast, clean lap". That is a
sparse, delayed signal — you learn nothing until the lap ends, and a policy that crashes at turn one
never sees it. **Reward shaping replaces it with a dense per-step surrogate**: a reward the agent can
follow gradient on at every timestep.

The risk is the whole subject. A surrogate reward is a *hypothesis* about what fast driving is made
of, and the agent will optimise the surrogate, not the intent. Shaping terms that reward speed
produce a car that goes fast into a wall; terms that reward staying centred produce a car that never
takes a racing line.

## Four formulations, one algorithm

Six of the eight experiment branches are reward experiments — the algorithm is held constant while
the reward is varied. That is the structure of [[branch-per-experiment]], and it is what makes the
branch reports readable as an experiment log rather than a changelog. The distinct formulations
documented with pseudocode across `docs/branch-reports/`:

| Formulation | The hypothesis |
|---|---|
| **Straightness / progress** | reward longitudinal progress along the track axis, penalise lateral drift and heading error |
| **Danger — time-to-edge** | reward is a function of *how long until you leave the track at the current heading and speed*, so the penalty arrives before the crash rather than at it |
| **RPM band** | reward holding the engine in its torque band — superseded by measurement in [[data-driven-gearing-over-hand-tuned-rpm-bands]] |
| **Jerk** | penalise the derivative of acceleration to suppress the oscillation the speed rewards produced |

The `stable` tree — the one that shipped — uses the **danger** formulation, with
`off_track_penalty = 10000.0` dominating everything else, plus `target_speed = 360`,
`corner_speed = 120` and `brake_enable_speed = 80.0` as the speed-shaping terms. The intent recorded
for it is learning *when to brake* without hand-coded braking zones.

Time-to-edge is the interesting one: it converts a discrete terminal event into a continuous quantity
the policy can see coming, which is exactly what shaping is supposed to do.

## What the reports record about the experiments failing

The branch reports are unusually honest about negative results — see
[[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]]. Two of the branch names do not describe their contents:

> "Despite the branch name, the tip commit contains **no reward-function code change**. The only"
> — IT Applications in Business and Commerce/project/docs/branch-reports/Reward_func_improvement.md, 2026-07-10

> "- A `calculate_jerk_reward` method exists (from the gear lineage) but is **commented out** of"
> — IT Applications in Business and Commerce/project/docs/branch-reports/headless.md, 2026-07-10

A shaping term that was written, tried and commented out is a **dead end that survived** — the branch
report preserves it where the code alone would show only an absence.
